summary.text: In the prime case, \(\phi(F_{33})=2^{2^{33}}\), while the general bound \(\phi(m)<m\) makes \(F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1\) minimal. In the composite case, a 2-adic factorization gives the required lower bound for even \(m\); for an odd \(m\) below that bound, its size forces every prime divisor to be a Fermat prime \(F_j\), and excluding \(F_{33}\) leaves \(j\le 32\), whose distinct totient valuations sum to at most \(\sum_{j=0}^{32}2^j=2^{33}-1\), contradicting the required valuation \(2^{33}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=2^N+1,
\]
and define
\[
a(N)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_{>0}:2^N\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
We prove that
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
The set in this minimum is nonempty, since
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N.
\]
Thus it is enough in each case to exhibit the claimed number and prove that no smaller positive integer has totient divisible by \(2^N\).

We use two preliminary lower bounds.

First, suppose \(b>0\) and \(2^N\mid\varphi(b)\). Since \(N\ge1\), we have \(2^N\ge2\). Divisibility and positivity of \(\varphi(b)\) imply
\[
2^N\le \varphi(b).
\]
The integer \(b\) cannot be \(1\), because \(\varphi(1)=1\). Hence \(b\ge2\), and the standard strict bound for the totient gives \(\varphi(b)<b\). Consequently
\[
2^N<b. \tag{1}
\]

We can strengthen this when \(b\) is even. Write
\[
b=2^\alpha d,
\]
where \(\alpha\ge1\) and \(d\) is odd. Since \(2^\alpha\) and \(d\) are coprime, multiplicativity of the totient gives
\[
\varphi(b)=\varphi(2^\alpha)\varphi(d)=2^{\alpha-1}\varphi(d).
\]
Let
\[
e=v_2(\varphi(d)),
\]
so that \(\varphi(d)=2^e u\) for an odd positive integer \(u\). It follows that
\[
\varphi(b)=2^{\alpha-1+e}u.
\]
Because \(u\) is odd, the condition \(2^N\mid\varphi(b)\) forces
\[
N\le \alpha-1+e,
\]
or equivalently
\[
N+1\le\alpha+e. \tag{2}
\]
Also \(2^e\mid\varphi(d)\), so
\[
2^e\le\varphi(d)\le d.
\]
Combining this with (2), we obtain
\[
2^{N+1}\le2^{\alpha+e}=2^\alpha 2^e\le2^\alpha d=b. \tag{3}
\]
Thus every even positive integer whose totient is divisible by \(2^N\) is at least \(2^{N+1}\).

We next prove the key assertion needed for odd integers.

**Key assertion.** If \(F_{33}\) is not prime, there is no odd positive integer \(m<2^{N+1}\) such that \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\).

Assume, for contradiction, that such an \(m\) exists. Let \(P\) be the set of distinct prime divisors of \(m\), and put
\[
R=\prod_{p\in P}p,
\qquad
Q=\prod_{p\in P}(p-1),
\qquad
O=\frac mR.
\]
If \(m=\prod_{p\in P}p^{\alpha_p}\), then
\[
O=\prod_{p\in P}p^{\alpha_p-1}.
\]
The prime-power formula for Euler's totient therefore gives
\[
\varphi(m)
 =\prod_{p\in P}p^{\alpha_p-1}(p-1)
 =OQ. \tag{4}
\]
Because \(m\) is odd, every prime in \(P\), and hence \(O\), is odd. Thus \(O\) is coprime to \(2^N\). From \(2^N\mid OQ\) and (4), Euclid's lemma gives
\[
2^N\mid Q. \tag{5}
\]

For every \(p\in P\), define
\[
t_p=v_2(p-1),
\qquad
c_p=\frac{p-1}{2^{t_p}}.
\]
Thus \(c_p\) is the positive odd part of \(p-1\), and
\[
p-1=2^{t_p}c_p.
\]
Since \(Q\) is the product of the nonzero integers \(p-1\), its \(2\)-adic valuation is the sum of their valuations. Condition (5) consequently implies
\[
N\le \sum_{p\in P}t_p. \tag{6}
\]
Let
\[
C=\prod_{p\in P}c_p.
\]
Multiplying the identities \(p-1=2^{t_p}c_p\) gives
\[
2^{\sum_{p\in P}t_p}C
 =\prod_{p\in P}(p-1)
 \le\prod_{p\in P}p
 =R.
\]
Moreover, \(R\mid m\), so \(R\le m\). Using (6), we therefore have
\[
2^N C
 \le 2^{\sum_{p\in P}t_p}C
 \le R
 \le m
 <2^{N+1}=2^N\cdot2.
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(2^N\) yields
\[
C<2.
\]
But \(C\) is a positive integer, so \(C=1\). Every \(c_p\) is a positive integer and their product is \(1\); hence
\[
c_p=1
\quad\text{for every }p\in P.
\]
It follows that every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) has the form
\[
p=2^{t_p}+1. \tag{7}
\]
Since \(m\) is odd, \(p\) is an odd prime. Therefore \(p\ne2\), so \(p-1\) is divisible by \(2\), and thus
\[
t_p\ge1. \tag{8}
\]

We now use the elementary fact that if \(t>0\) and \(2^t+1\) is prime, then \(t\) is a power of \(2\). To see this, write
\[
t=2^j u
\]
with \(u\) odd. If \(u>1\), let \(x=2^{2^j}\). Then
\[
2^t+1=x^u+1.
\]
Because \(u>1\) is odd, \(x+1\) divides \(x^u+1\). Furthermore,
\[
1<x+1<x^u+1,
\]
so \(x^u+1\) would be composite. Hence \(u=1\), proving \(t=2^j\).

Applying this fact to (7) and (8), for each \(p\in P\) there is an integer \(j_p\ge0\) such that
\[
t_p=2^{j_p}
\quad\text{and}\quad
p=2^{2^{j_p}}+1. \tag{9}
\]
We next bound \(j_p\). Since \(p\mid m\) and \(m>0\), we have \(p\le m\). By hypothesis, \(m<2^{N+1}\). Therefore (9) gives
\[
2^{2^{j_p}}<2^{2^{j_p}}+1=p\le m<2^{N+1}.
\]
Strict monotonicity of powers of \(2\) implies
\[
2^{j_p}<N+1.
\]
Both sides are integers, so \(2^{j_p}\le N=2^{33}\), and hence
\[
j_p\le33. \tag{10}
\]
If \(j_p=33\), then (9) would say
\[
p=2^{2^{33}}+1=F_{33}.
\]
But \(p\) is prime, contradicting the present assumption that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. Thus in fact
\[
0\le j_p\le32. \tag{11}
\]

The values \(t_p\) for distinct primes \(p\in P\) are distinct. Indeed, (7) says \(p=2^{t_p}+1\), so equality \(t_p=t_q\) immediately implies \(p=q\). Therefore the collection \(\{t_p:p\in P\}\) is a set of distinct elements selected from
\[
\{2^0,2^1,\ldots,2^{32}\}
\]
by (9) and (11). It follows that
\[
\sum_{p\in P}t_p
\le \sum_{j=0}^{32}2^j
=2^{33}-1. \tag{12}
\]
The last equality is the usual finite geometric-sum identity, obtained for example by induction from
\(\sum_{j=0}^{r}2^j=2^{r+1}-1\).

On the other hand, (6) and \(N=2^{33}\) say
\[
2^{33}=N\le\sum_{p\in P}t_p.
\]
Together with (12), this gives
\[
2^{33}\le2^{33}-1,
\]
an impossibility. This proves the key assertion.

We now finish by separating the two cases in the statement.

Suppose first that \(F_{33}\) is prime. Since
\[
F_{33}=2^N+1,
\]
we have
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=2^N.
\]
Thus \(F_{33}\) belongs to the defining set for \(a(N)\). Conversely, every member \(b\) of that set satisfies the general lower bound (1):
\[
2^N<b.
\]
As \(b\) is an integer, this implies
\[
b\ge2^N+1=F_{33}.
\]
Hence \(F_{33}\) is the least member, and
\[
a(N)=F_{33}.
\]

Finally, suppose that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. We already observed that
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N,
\]
so \(2^{N+1}\) belongs to the defining set. Let \(b>0\) satisfy \(2^N\mid\varphi(b)\). If \(b\) is even, the strengthened lower bound (3) gives
\[
b\ge2^{N+1}.
\]
If \(b\) is odd and were smaller than \(2^{N+1}\), it would contradict the key assertion. Hence in the odd case as well,
\[
b\ge2^{N+1}.
\]
Thus every member of the defining set is at least \(2^{N+1}\), while \(2^{N+1}\) itself is a member. Therefore
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}=2^{2^{33}+1}.
\]

Substituting \(N=2^{33}\) proves precisely
\[
a(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1\text{ is prime},\\
2^{2^{33}+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
